title: Parenting in lockdown: Coronavirus and the effects on work-life balance
meta_description: Parents in the UK have been fitting in work commitments around childcare during the first weeks of the pandemic

breadcrumb.text: Parenting in lockdown: Coronavirus and the effects on work-life balance

lede: Parents in Great Britain who have been able to work through the coronavirus lockdown have adapted their working patterns around caring for their children. There were some clear trends in how that childcare was delivered.

body.text: 22 July 2020
Lockdown in the UK has presented challenges for families whose day-to-day lives were transformed virtually overnight.

At the start of the lockdown (23 March 2020), many people had to rapidly adjust to a ‘new normal’, with school closures, parents furloughed or working from home, and support from outside the home no longer available.
For millions of parents (or those in a parenting role), this included having to care for their children, including homeschooling them, while continuing to work.

A separate bulletin on [homeschooling](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/coronavirusandhomeschoolingingreatbritainapriltojune2020) in Great Britain, offers insight into the challenges faced by those school closures.

body.h3: Parents fitted in work commitments around childcare
body.text: Parents fitted in work commitments around childcare

body.h3: Parents fitted in work commitments around childcare
body.text: Analysis of time use data has shown that many parents in Great Britain who were able to work, changed their routines to accommodate their new childcare commitments, prompted by the coronavirus (COVID-19) lockdown.

body.h3: Parents fitted in work commitments around childcare
body.text: For working parents with school-aged children that said their work had been affected by the coronavirus, 20% said this disruption was at least in part because of having to work around childcare responsibilities.

body.h3: Parents fitted in work commitments around childcare
body.text: During the lockdown, [parents were nearly twice as likely to be furloughed (13.6%) as those without children (7.2%).](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/bulletins/personalandeconomicwellbeingintheuk/june2020) This is one example of the added complications for families of the restrictions.

body.h3: Parents fitted in work commitments around childcare
body.text: Those parents who worked outside of the home contributed childcare outside the usual ‘nine to five’ hours, which suggests that they were more likely to be working unsociable hours.

body.h3: The type of childcare that was provided changed during lockdown
body.h4: During lockdown, parents spent more time on developmental childcare
body.h5: Notes:
body.text: There has been a marked change in the type of unpaid childcare provided overall, between 2015 and 2020.

body.h3: The type of childcare that was provided changed during lockdown
body.h4: During lockdown, parents spent more time on developmental childcare
body.h5: Notes:
body.text: In this analysis, childcare1 has been defined as developmental (such as helping with school work) and non-developmental (such as dressing children).

body.h3: The type of childcare that was provided changed during lockdown
body.h4: During lockdown, parents spent more time on developmental childcare
body.h5: Notes:
body.text: There was a 32% drop in the average time spent per day on providing non-developmental childcare, which also includes getting ready for school and going out for recreation. Between 2015 and 2020 this declined from 56 to 38 minutes a day.

body.h3: The type of childcare that was provided changed during lockdown
body.h4: During lockdown, parents spent more time on developmental childcare
body.h5: Notes:
body.text: This change is likely to be because daily life under lockdown was different from the norm; people were being advised to stay at home and public spaces and recreational facilities were closed.

body.h3: The type of childcare that was provided changed during lockdown
body.h4: During lockdown, parents spent more time on developmental childcare
body.h5: Notes:
body.text: Meanwhile the amount of time devoted to developmental childcare, such as helping with homework and homeschooling, increased by 169%, from 24 to 64 minutes a day.

body.h3: Women have carried out more childcare duties overall
body.text: Women have carried out more childcare duties overall

body.h3: Women have carried out more childcare duties overall
body.text: During the first weeks of lockdown (28 March to 26 April 2020), in households with children aged under 18 years, women were carrying out on average two-thirds more of the childcare duties per day than men.

body.h3: Women have carried out more childcare duties overall
body.text: Women were delivering an average of 3 hours and 18 minutes of childcare, which includes time spent supervising children, while men contributed 2 hours.

body.h3: Footnotes:
body.text: Footnotes:

body.h3: Footnotes:
body.text: Developmental childcare: includes activities where caregivers are undertaking activities with the aim to develop a child’s cognitive development. This may include activities such as reading to children, playing with children or helping children with their school work.Non-developmental childcare: includes all the other tasks. These other tasks also have a welfare focus but are more concerned with physical care tasks such as feeding, washing or dressing children.All childcare: is either developmental or non-developmental childcare, plus additional time where respondents reported being responsible for children in a supervisory capacity.

body.h3: Footnotes:
body.text: The learning referred to in the bulletin [Coronavirus and homeschooling in Great Britain, April to June 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/coronavirusandhomeschoolingingreatbritainapriltojune2020) concerns how many hours of learning a child has done using online lessons, worksheets or other materials provided by their teachers, whetherwith their parents or not, and how both parents have felt about the experience.The learning referred to in this release captures supervised learning, such as help with homework.

body.h3: Footnotes:
body.text: While they address similar themes, the publications use different sources, time periods and definitions, Parenting in lockdown: this release uses the online time use survey, while [Coronavirus and homeschooling in Great Britain, April to June 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/coronavirusandhomeschoolingingreatbritainapriltojune2020) uses the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN).
